utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Everyone might have expected that we would start to deal with the Treanor exhibits, but since there is a problem with the computers, I'd rather delay that until everything is functioning fully, so that the Registry can file, or at least can register all the necessary numbers, et cetera, in a proper way. That means that we could then continue with your next witness, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm Thomas Hannis, on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I should do that at the beginning of the week to see who is there. Whenever I see any new faces. I see that the Prosecution is supported by or at least there's some other person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the new face to my immediate left is Mr. Willem Wijermars, who is from our trial support unit and will be appearing on occasion to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Well, the Defence is still the same as usual: Mr. Stewart, Ms. Loukas, and Ms. Cmeric. Now your next witness will be a 92 bis witness and I take it you'll introduce that witness in a way as we usually do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that Judge Canivell has an earphone but doesn't hear anything. Let's just check whether it properly functions. Yes. I'll say a few words, Judge Canivell, so that you can test your ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This problem having been solved, your next witness will be, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our first witness this morning will be Mr. Mustafa Ramic, whose evidence is sought to be admitted pursuant to 92 bis and then the Court had ordered that he appear for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Ramic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ramic. Before giving evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will be handed out to you now in your own language. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ramic. Please be seated. Mr. Ramic, you have given earlier statements and you have already testified in this Tribunal. That means that the emphasis today will be on questions to be put to you by the Defence. But first, Mr. Hannis of the Prosecution will introduce you as a witness before you'll be examined by the Defence. Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This witness previously testified in this Tribunal in the Jelisic and the Milosevic cases. In addition, pursuant to 92 -- Rule 92 bis, we had sought the admission of both those testimonies and testimony from his prior statements to the ICTY. I would like to read briefly, fairly briefly, a summary of what we believe that evidence is. Mustafa Ramic was heavily involved in the formation of the SDA in Brcko in 1990. The witness explains in earlier testimony that the SDA came in second in the 1990 multi-party elections, with 23 seats. The SDP, or Communist Party, won the majority of seats in the Brcko municipal parliament. They were a mixed group, that is, there were Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats amongst them. After the election, there was a coalition set up by the SDA, HDZ, and SDS. The Executive Council comprised three SDA, three HDZ, and three SDS members. This witness describes the various posts in the municipal government occupied on a parity basis by Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. The highest-ranking position was occupied by the witness. He was president of the Brcko Municipal Assembly. For several months before the war broke out, the JNA was distributing weapons among the Serb population in villages in Brcko municipality. There was a noticeable increase in military activity and an increased number of troops at the JNA barracks in the town of Brcko. The witness telephoned the JNA commander, Lieutenant Colonel Pavle Milinkovic repeatedly about what was happening. He also went to see him to ask why tanks were digging in and why groups with machine-guns deployed around the town. It was particularly odd that most of these weapons were aimed towards the town. Milinkovic would not discuss it. He would say from time to time that these activities were being conducted also as a defence against incursion of some foreign forces from Croatia. The witness proposed a joint unit made up of Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, but this was refused. The SDS wanted to partition the town into separate areas, with Serbs getting control of a significant portion of the downtown and industrial areas of Brcko. This was debated at a televised parliamentary session on about the 27th of April, 1992. At an earlier meeting with some SDS officials, the witness was warned that if the Serb demands were not accepted, bad things would happen in Brcko. The witness describes an occasion in which he and his brother questioned Dr. Milenko Vojinovic, also known as Dr. Beli, SDS Main Board member and Brcko representative to the Bosnian Serb National Assembly, about why the SDS was insisting on a Serb municipality of Brcko and division of the town. Dr. Beli told the witness that Dr. Radovan Karadzic and the SDS leadership required this of him. In a subsequent conversation, Dr. Beli told the witness that if the proposed division of the town was not accepted, then it would be carried out by force. The SDA's position was that the proposed division of the town was unacceptable, but because of the Serbs' control of the local JNA, the police, and the Territorial Defence, the SDA reluctantly agreed to SDS demands in hopes of avoiding bloodshed. All three parties took part in the debate, and the matter was continued for further discussion at another meeting to be held on 4 May 1992. By the 1st of May, 1992, after the bridges in Brcko were destroyed, there was not a single bridge across the Sava River by which one could go to Croatia. Two bridges were blown up in Brcko: The railway bridge, and the bridge for vehicles and pedestrians. The railway bridge was blown up within three minutes of the pedestrian bridge. The blowing of the bridges caused panic in the town and large numbers of people began to leave. This witness had ordered that the pedestrian bridge be protected. A group of policemen had been set up as a checkpoint there. They later told the witness that the people who had blown up the bridge were very well prepared, that they numbered about 20, and that they were from Serbia. These men had taken over the checkpoint and waited until morning to activate the explosives. About 150 civilians were on the bridge at the time. After the bridges were blown up, the witness says that he went to a meeting with JNA Lieutenant Colonel Milinkovic at the Brcko barracks. Milinkovic said that he would bring the army in to take control of all the important points in town. Mr. Ramic asked to keep the JNA out and allow the civilian police to handle law and order. Milinkovic said that he would agree not to bring in the army if the witness would go on television and succeeded in calming the people down. The witness agreed to do so and he was escorted to the TV station and attended there by the JNA assistant commander for security matters, Captain Momcilo Petrovic, during that broadcast. People telephoned in and said that the army was already entering the town. At one point, people phoned up from a local community called 4th of July and said: "The army is at present shooting at us." The witness asked the deputy commander of the garrison what this meant, given that the army had agreed not to enter the town. The programme was interrupted and the witness left the television studio. He has testified that he thought if he had stayed, the Serbs would probably have killed him. The witness went ultimately to Gornji Rahic, which was located in free Brcko. He spent most of his time there during the war. When an attack was launched by the JNA and paramilitary units, he organised the defence of the rest of the town. They succeeded in controlling part of the town and the southern areas. This witness has produced and verified several documents in his prior testimonies, including a list of names of prominent Muslims killed during the first days in May 1992 in Brcko and whose bodies were found in mass grave sites in the Brcko area; organisational charts showing the division of power between the three national parties in Brcko; and a list showing the structure and ethnic composition of the local police and Territorial Defence. The evidence of this witness, Your Honours, is relevant to paragraphs 4 through 8, 15 through 19, and 24, and also to counts 1 through 6 of the indictment. Your Honour, that concludes my reading of the summary, and I have no question for the witness at this time, and proffer him for

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Mr. Ramic, you'll now be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just to check that I'm near enough to the microphone for everybody. Otherwise I'll have to move it or myself. If there's no problem, then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, can you tell the Tribunal about an incident at a village called Sijekovac in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say you're not aware what it's about, do you mean that you know literally nothing whatever of what it's about?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Well, there is no village of Sijekovac in the municipality of Brcko. Are you sure you read out the name of the village correctly? That's the first reason. And second, I don't know which incident you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sijekovac. Does that sound right to you as the name of a village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I believe I've heard the name of the village somewhere, but I was the president of the Brcko municipality, and I'm familiar with this particular municipality. There is no village of Sijekovac in the municipality of Brcko. Maybe there is a part of the village with a different name. Are you referring to the village of Bijela or Bukvik or Vitanovici. Could it be one of those villages?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm referring to the village of Sijekovac, which is in Bosanski Brod. Do you know that village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No. No. That's exactly what I'm talking about. Bosanski Brod is a different municipality. This is not part of the Brcko municipality in respect of which I can give testimony. As for Bosanski Brod, you're referring to the overall war events. I thought you were talking to a particular village in the Brcko municipality. Now I understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, you've come here to give testimony on whatever you know, whether it is within or outside of Brcko municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you're asked whether you know a village Sijekovac, then please tell us whether you know of the existence, wherever it is, whether it's Brcko or not. You're asked about an incident in a certain village. If you know that village or if you know about the incident, please tell Mr. Stewart, and if you are not familiar even with the existence of the village, then say: I do not know whether such a village exists. Yes. Is that clear? Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With those ground rules, if I may put it that way, from His Honour, Mr. Ramic, perhaps we'll just start again. Have you heard of a village called Sijekovac in Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And have you ever heard anything about an incident which occurred in that village, or around that village, in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I think you are referring to the plight of the Serbian population in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, I am, I hope with His Honour's support as necessary here, I'm going to attempt also to try and have some ground rules between us. Mr. Ramic, if you stop speculating about what I am doing and what the point of my questions is, and if you confine yourself strictly to what His Honour asked you to do, which is to answer my questions, then we shall make much more rapid and effective progress. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever heard anything about an incident which occurred in that village, or around that village, in early 1992, the village in question being Sijekovac?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what incident you are referring to. You have to give me a few more hints.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you know about any incident, tell us about the incident you know about. If you say: I know about three incidents, tell us which three, and from the next questions, it will be clear to you what incident Mr. Stewart is specifically interested in, but tell us what you know. So do you know about one or more incidents that you're aware of took place in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this moment, I can't recall any specific incident that took place in Sijekovac village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say not a specific incident, what do you know about an incident or incidents having taken place in that village? We'd like to know what you do know, not what you do not know. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat: I am not sure that I can say anything specific about any incident which took place in Sijekovac village.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, I discourage you from doing it, but you said -- one of your answers to this question, that you thought I was referring to the plight of the Serbs in that village. Mr. Ramic, it does appear that you do know something about an incident in that village. Please will you tell the Tribunal what you know.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, a little while ago, I tried to say what I think. However, the Defence counsel has discouraged me from doing that, and that's why I'm saying that I don't know exactly what this incident this is about. But I believe that this had to do with the plight of the Serbian citizens in that area. I did hear about the plight of the Serbian population in that area. This is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, I don't want to have to play games or have a debate with you, but you are trying to be clever here. You said that I discouraged you from saying what you thought. Mr. Ramic, let's make it absolutely clear. I discouraged you from saying what I, Nicholas Stewart, thought. That's a completely different thing. Can we stick to what you're here to do, which is you to answer my questions. But since you seem to be so reluctant, I will give you a little bit of help. I suggest to you that there was an incident in the village of Sijekovac, in Bosanski Brod, in late February 1992, involving an attack on the village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've been asked about this before, haven't you, in giving evidence before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, and my answer was similar. I said that I thought that there might have been an attack on the Serbian village, but I don't have the exact information about this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, give us the information you have. You can't give any information you don't have, but you seem to have information. Give us the information you have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you have to allow me a moment to describe what I know. What I know is as follows: I know that in that area, in Brod municipality, that is, Bosanski Brod municipality, there were conflicts and clashes, and that there were attacks on Croatian villages, as well as on Serbian villages. As far as I remember at this moment, Sijekovac was a Serbian village, and at one point in time, it came under attack, and I think that there was a number of killings committed there. But I have to tell Your Honours that this is what I heard from other people, and I don't have the exact information, the exact data about those events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would have given this answer at the first question of Mr. Stewart, we would have saved 15 to 20 minutes, because it's entirely clear to us now that you have, although secondhand knowledge of events that happened over there. Could you please, for the next question of Mr. Stewart, give him the answer right away. Whether it's a pleasant answer or not is not the main issue. Whether it's good for whomever is not the issue. Just tell us what you know, whether you heard it from someone, whether you saw it yourself. Just tell us what you know, and we'll move on far better than we did until now. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, what do you know about the formation of the 108th Brigade of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, and specifically, the 3rd Company of the 108th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: The 108th Brigade is a brigade which was established in the territory of Brcko municipality. It was established on the 17th of May, 1992. 17 days after the beginning of war, or the aggression against the town of Brcko. As far as the 3rd Company is concerned, the brigade was divided into battalions, and when you say the 3rd Company, I am thinking now in order to be able to decide what formation are you referring to. Can you please be more precise in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll ask you a different question. Who is or was Rasid Guso.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Rasid Guso was one of the fighters in the 108th Brigade. I believe that he was the commander of this 3rd Company. I believe he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Wasn't he in fact the commander of a special Muslim unit within that brigade?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: He was a well-known fighter. And as far as I can remember now, he was the commander of a company, and I believe that the company was that precise company. I don't know, I'm not sure that he was the commander of a special unit, but in any case, he was a very well-known fighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So is the position as far as you know that he might have been the commander of a special Muslim unit or he might not, but you personally simply don't know?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: He might have been, yes. I will allow that. He might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you know him personally in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How well?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Before the war, I didn't know him at all. During the war, I got to know him as much as one could get to know a fighter during such events. I knew him as a fighter. I didn't know him as a private individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you know him as a fighter before the blowing up of the bridge at Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Your question is not clear to me. There were no fighters before the bridge was blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you know him before the blowing up of the bridge at Brcko on the 30th of April/1st of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know who Blaz Lovric is?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He also had a name Baja, Baja. Does that jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This does ring a bell. He was also a well-known fighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was he the commander of a special Croat unit within the 108th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I apologise for having to say it once again, that I am not sure, but he might have been. I'll allow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know that there were, in fact, whoever was -- were commanders, there were in fact a special Muslim unit and a special Croat unit within the 108th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: There were no special units. There were so-called intervention platoons. And if you are referring to those units, then the answer is yes. In any case, we called those units intervention platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What did that mean, the title "intervention platoon"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: One could say that those units had a special purpose. They were called to deal with very special situations, for example, when the situation on the front line was especially dire, they would be sent there to deal with the situation. So those units were sent to deal with special situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 11th of June, 1992, a Serb village of Bosanska Bijela was attacked by members of the 108th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I can give some answer with this regard, but let me first correct you. It could not have been an attack, because Bosanska Bijela was under the control of the 108th Brigade. It was under their control, and there was no special reason to attack the village. Secondly, this village, Bosanska Bijela, was predominantly a Catholic village. 70 per cent of the villagers were Catholic and 30 per cent of the villagers were Serbs. However, during that period, there was an incident in that village, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was that incident? Please describe it in the first place, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I think that there was a clash between the parts. I believe that the intention was to disarm the Serbian population, who had weapons during that period of time, and that this resulted in a clash.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you remember that about 20 Serb civilians were killed by members of the 108th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: There were casualties. I don't know what their number was, and I don't know who the dead people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, going back a bit, then, to when the -- there was the outbreak of hostilities in Brcko at the end of April and very beginning of May 1992. You, Mr. Ramic, were the head of the Defence Council, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the name of the body, the Defence Council. It was an institution of the government in the then-Bosnia-Herzegovina or its municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you've told this Tribunal before that when the -- this is your evidence, that when the shooting started and the attack on Brcko - that was your evidence - was launched by army and paramilitary units, that you organised the defence of the rest of the town. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you said you succeeded in controlling part of the town and the southern reaches. And "you" here means the Muslim community, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I would say that this was the other way around. I can't answer your question, because it is not precise, and my answer cannot be the answer to your question. Brcko came under attack. There was aggression against Brcko. I was the representative of the legal bodies of government and I was not the one to place the town under control. I was defending it, and one could say that at that moment, we managed to defend one part of the town, and that would be my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, let's be more specific, then. When in your previous evidence you said - and this was in the case against Mr. Jelisic - you said: We succeeded in controlling part of the town and the southern reaches. And that's just -- for everybody's reference, that's at page 1741 of the transcript in that case. When you say, "We succeeded in controlling part of the town and the southern reaches," can you tell this Tribunal specifically who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: When I say "we," I'm referring to the representatives of the then-legal government of the town of Brcko, the legal authorities. And I'm referring to myself, the police, and the Territorial Defence that we had at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let us try and be realistic, Mr. Ramic. Was anybody who was included in "we" for these purposes not a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Of course. There were Croats as well as Bosniak Muslims. But I would like to tell you another thing. When I say "we," I'm also referring to a number of Serbs. There were not many Serbs, but there were Serbs among us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: At this moment, I can't remember exactly, but there must have been anything between five and ten of them. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Out of a total number included in "we"? Total number of how many?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I cannot speak about the total number at this moment. The war line was established at that time. On the one side of that line were Muslim Bosniak and Catholic villages, as well as two Serbian villages. So when I say "we," I'm referring to that area. And now, as for the number of people who defended that line, there must have been several hundreds of such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in order to control part of the town and the southern reaches, as you described it, you must have had, I suggest to you, at least a solid foundation of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Not exactly. We did not have enough weapons. We were not well armed. We did have weapons, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'd like you to be as specific as you can, Mr. Ramic, about the extent of the weaponry in the hands of the -- I think several hundred that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I would like to say this. There were several hundreds of people, but they did not have weapons. The following would happen: On the front line, we had teams with weapons. They would be replaced by other teams who would then take over their weapons. So not everybody had weapons. Now, if you are asking me about the weapons, those were private hunting rifles. There were people who had licences to carry weapons for their private individual needs. There were also police officers who had their official weapons, and there were also members of the Territorial Defence who had weapons belonging to the Territorial Defence. This is the weapons that I am referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So were there several -- I assume they were men for practical purposes. Were there several hundred men who each had at least some weapon?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So can you say roughly how many included in your description of "we" that controlled part of the town, how many, from your recollection, had their own weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: At that moment, at the beginning of war, I can't give you the exact number. I can give you an approximate number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: It was less than a hundred people who had weapons. Less than a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were you able to acquire any further weapons within, let us say, the first two weeks of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we did acquire some. In the course of May, we did acquire some infantry weapons. I'm referring to automatic rifles and semi-automatic rifles. We also acquired at the very beginning of May about a hundred such pieces of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where did you get them from?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: We got them through an urgent intervention via our friends in Croatia. We didn't get it through official channels, from the Croatian government or the Croatian army. We got them from our friends in Croatia, with the help of some people from Brcko municipality who had gone to Croatia to search for weapons, to find weapons, and buy weapons. We had a group of people from Brcko who went to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was that group in operation, in the way that you've just described, before the end of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How quickly do you say it was formed after the 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: This group was dispatched urgently, on the second day. The aggression against the town took place on the 1st of May, and this group of people was dispatched to search for weapons on the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So let's get it straight. The group was then formed on the 1st or 2nd of May and dispatched on the 2nd of May? That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How large was this group?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: There were three people, three men in this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what were their names?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not wish to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Maybe we should go into private session for this. If it's necessary. Your Honour, and at this point I guess I should say I'm not sure I see the relevance of this line of testimony at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the first question is whether this question should be answered in open session or in closed session. And the second question, if you could answer that without influencing the witness in such a way, that's the relevance question. You could do it in his presence. If you think, however - and I rely on your fair judgement - that you should do it in the absence of the witness, we could ask the witness to leave the courtroom for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't think I have a problem, Your Honour. The two questions, I might myself put them logically the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course they're not related but they come up at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the question for me to answer is the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the question for you to answer. The other is whether we -- when you're asking the witness to answer your previous question, whether it should be done in open or in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm perfectly happy to deal with this. So far as the relevance is concerned, that is very simple. The Defence wishes entirely legitimately to have such information as it can get in relation to these that the witness knows, and it is entirely legitimate for us to ask him to give such information so that we may pursue lines of inquiry, if necessary. That's a perfectly legitimate element of cross-examination. Leaving aside the second question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The answer to this question, as you've just given it to us, would be valid on whatever question one would ask a witness about facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That means that there would be no limit as far as relevance is concerned any more because this answer would always be valid if -- to the full extent supported by the Chamber to put a question to a witness, because it could always be a source for further inquiries. Before -- let me just confer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I add something first, Your Honour, to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With respect. Well, yes, what Your Honour says is perfectly true. It does have this protection, Your Honour, which is not trivial. These questions are in the hands of professional advocates who are not simply asking completely irrelevant questions just for the fun of it and that is something on which the Tribunal is entitled to place and should place very significant reliance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although it should not be the final answer to relevance or not. Otherwise, the Bench had an easy task.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not suggesting the Bench abdicates or hands over its responsibility, but it is a very important element.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will not prevent the witness this answer on the basis of relevance. It's also -- I think you justly asked some confidence from the Chamber, the Chamber gives it to you. It's also in your hands to keep the Chamber to be confident in the professionality of counsel. Should the question be perhaps better be answered in closed session, or at least in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, so far as that is concerned, it's always slightly difficult here. One possibility is to go quickly into closed session to explore why it needs to be in closed session. But it may be, in order -- because that does take a certain amount of time. It seems to me that it's perfectly safe to ask the witness, in very general terms, the witness himself realising that we are in open session, to give some indication as to why the withholding of these men's names requires closed session. Because we've explored this before. There clearly must be some solid reason given before we go into closed session. I suggest that's a suitable course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it's up for a witness to give the solid reason or to express his doubts, whether he could answer a question in open or in private session is a different matter. May I ask you, Witness, Mr. Ramic: You were asked to give the names of those who were in the group who tried to get weapons abroad. Are you willing to give the names of these persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have to understand me. I would have to have the consent of the people involved, because they're still alive. And for reasons of their safety, of the safety of their lives today, I do not wish to tell you their names in an open session. However, if you insist, I can give you the names in a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again. The Chamber has heard part of the testimony of the witness in private session. There has been some argument on whether it was appropriate to hear all this evidence in private session. The Chamber has considered the matter and decided that it should not be kept from the public, that among those persons who were seeking weapons abroad was your brother, but leave it to that and give no further information. The Chamber has to balance the impact on the public character of the trial, on the one hand, and of course also keeps in mind to what extent the Defence will be deprived from its facilities to further inquiry into certain matters. Of course, private session does not prohibit the Defence from further inquiring into matters, because even if protective measures were granted, then, to the extent necessary for the preparation of the defence, of course, the Defence may operate with those data. Of course, on the other hand of the balance is the risk for persons, and if we are talking about the protection of a witness, a witness himself put forward what in his view is of importance in relation to his protection. Whereas if we're talking about third parties, they are not in a position to present themselves here in Court. And the Chamber is also aware that if you make mistakes in this respect, that it could have disastrous consequences. For that reason, the Chamber has decided to proceed cautiously in this respect. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. There would be a slight nuisance for which I apologise, because the Court has gone into open session again. But Ms. Cmeric tells me that we're not 100 per cent clear about one of those other names, anyway. It seems that there are two men with the same surname, so that we would need perhaps to go very briefly into private session just to clarify those names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ramic, could you perhaps please write down the two names of the other persons you gave, and it will then be given through the usher to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. That's perfectly satisfactory, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you'd please write them down and then, Mr. Stewart, we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may give it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, the evidence that you've given so far, then, is that this group of these three men, including your brother, Ibrahim, started to -- the exercise of obtaining weapons from Croatia on, I think you said, the 2nd of May. And how quickly did they manage to obtain those weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Approximately one week to ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And can you say what the nature and quantity of what weaponry was obtained?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: If my memory serves me right, we're talking about a hundred or so automatic rifles, about 50 pieces of smaller arms, pistols and little automatic weapons. And I also believe that there were some others. I'm not a hundred per cent sure, but I believe that there were some four or five mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So according to your evidence, it was around the -- it would have been around somewhere between perhaps the 9th and the 12th of May before that additional weaponry was obtained?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's about correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So when you referred in your evidence in the Jelisic case to: "We succeeded in controlling part of the town and the southern reaches," at what point in the chronology, at what point in April, May 1992 did you succeed in controlling part of the town and the southern regions?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I thought that you understood me the first time round. On the 1st of May, the war activities started. On the following day, they intensified. The separation line went through the town somewhere near the Brka River, and this is how the situation stayed for a few days. We were on the other side, and the aggressor was in the main part of the town. This is what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So just to get it clear, then: That success in controlling part of the town and the southern reaches was achieved very soon, within a day or so, after the blowing up of the bridges; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: If you will allow me. I have to answer the following way: I believe that it would be better to say that the aggressor did not achieve to cross the river and get to the other side. This would be a better way of putting it, rather than saying that we managed to gain control. We were there, and it was not up to us to gain control, because the control had never been taken away from us in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just to try and calm things down a little, Mr. Ramic. May I make it clear that the way of putting it, which you took some exception to a moment ago, was my quotation of your words in a previous case. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes, I'm clear about that. However, I can't remember exactly which words I used in the Jelisic case. However, I remember other things very well, and this is the only truth. We controlled the entire town. Then we lost control over half of the town, because the aggressor, the JNA, with other paramilitaries, gained control of that part of the town but never managed to cross the River Brka and reach the other part of the town that we had controlled all the time, and that is the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How would you describe the -- what are called the military situation -- I'll explain what I mean. Obviously you've got fighting sides. That's absolutely clear from your evidence. So from early May, during the first few days of May, clearly you've got groups fighting with each other. So that's what I'll call the military situation. At the point when you did acquire these additional weapons, you agree is probably sometime between the 9th and the 12th of May, how would you describe the military situation as it was then?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: The description of the situation would be as follows. From the 2nd of May up to the moment when we received the weapons, around the 10th of May, I was in charge of the defence of that part. However, it was my constant fear that we wouldn't manage to fend the attacks off on the following day. This is what the situation was at that time. We lived from one day to another, in fear that we wouldn't be able to defend ourselves. Every day, in the evening, when I reviewed the situation of the previous day and the operations on the front line, the ratio of the forces, and my conclusion every evening was that on the following day we wouldn't be able to defend ourselves any longer, up to the moment we finally received the weapons, and then the situation improved in our favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So at the point immediately before you received those extra weapons, let me put it this way: Supposing you were giving a military report on the situation at that point, briefly, what would you have said? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: In that case, let me give you a description. We were under attack by the complete JNA, which was stationed in the territory of Brcko municipality. Together with the JNA, there was a huge number of some other paramilitary formations. I knew that. I had information and I saw them with my own two eyes. There were Arkan's guard, who had come from Serbia. There were also the so-called White Eagles from Serbia as well. There were also members of the military formation of the Serbian Radical Party from Bijeljina, as well as some other Serbian volunteers. This was the force that had attacked us. On their strength, they had at that moment over ten tanks, in addition to other artillery. Also, according to my information, they had four or five artillery divisions at their disposal, and they were constantly shelling us from howitzers. They also had a number of mortars turned towards us. The number of soldiers who attacked us, I don't know exactly what their numbers were, but according to my estimate, there must have been over a thousand of them at the time. On the other hand, during the first couple of days, we managed to set up the defence line along the Brka River, which flows through the middle part of the town, dividing it into two parts, the south-west and the north-east. We were in the south-west part and we held this front line for two days. Then, obviously, they crossed with the tanks and they gradually pushed us from that part of the town and the defence line was slowly moving in their favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, you appear to have, on your evidence, you, that group that you described as "we," appear to have defended yourselves for some days against what you describe as very heavy forces of what you describe as the aggressor, when, according to your evidence, you had a total of about a hundred weapons, among which were hunting rifles. Could you perhaps explain what it was with such limited resources which enabled you to be at least relatively successful at that point in defending yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Kindly understand me when I say this: I did mention hunting rifles, but this was not the most important weaponry. I also said that there were weapons from the police, and the police officers who had them were Bosniaks and Croats. They had their police weapons. These were not hunting rifles. There were also parts of the Territorial Defence who at that moment managed to keep some of the weapons. Again, these were not hunting rifles. Secondly, during these first moments, the aggressor was so much more powerful that, according to my estimate, they showed arrogance in their approach. They thought that it would be easy to take the town. They suffered huge losses. However, because we ambushed them from behind the houses, and I believe that during these first couple of days, the aggressor suffered, according to my estimate, some 30 dead men, and this managed to stop them. It was then that they realised that it wouldn't be so easy, and they became more cautious, and they withdrew a little for a moment and then, after that, they treaded with caution and only with tank support and the support of armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Before the 1st of May, Mr. Ramic, was there any sort of group in action on attempting to obtain weapons in the way that you have described your brother and these two other men obtaining weapons after the 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: The group was organised by the municipality that I was the head of, or the Territorial Defence, did not exist before the 1st of May. However, I believe that there were individual attempts by people to arm themselves. During the last 10 or 15 days of April, people felt tension in the air. There was a state of chaos. There was a feeling of uncertainty. According to my information, some individuals tried to arm themselves at the time, but there were no organised groups set up to obtain weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You see, I'll make it clear what I'm getting at, Mr. Ramic. Evidence that you have given before this Tribunal, that you personally have given, is to the effect that, for some considerable time, weeks and possibly even going back months, there was great tension. You've described considerable fears among the Muslim community, to the extent that large numbers of the Muslim community actually left Brcko. You had shortly before the events of the 30th of April and the 1st of May, in fact, sent your own family to Zagreb. You have described your discussions with the JNA. You have given evidence of weaponry pointing towards Brcko. And against all that background, is it the case, Mr. Ramic, that there were more organised and concerted efforts and arrangements put in place by the Muslim community to obtain weaponry than you have so far told this Trial Chamber today?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. My answer is an explicit no. There was not an organised group who was involved in armament. Up to the 1st of May, everybody, including myself, hoped that there wouldn't be a war. We invested a lot of effort into preventing any conflicts. This was where our interests lay. We knew that we would never be able to arm ourselves so well to be able to stand up to the other side, which was the official armed force of that state.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you did acquire these extra weapons around the 9th to the 12th of May, how useful were they to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: At that moment, this was a decisive thing for our survival. At that moment, we realised that we would be able to hold for a while. With that weapons, we soon started organising our military structure. Seven days after that, we set up our first brigade, our first military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what did that achieve for you in practice?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: In practical terms, this meant the following: All able-bodied men in the territory of Brcko municipality under our control were involved in military formations, either directly as fighters or in other ways. Secondly, when this unit was established, we managed to establish a link with the military system of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And thirdly, when this unit was established, we reached an agreement with the Croatian part of the population, who were also involved, and thus we managed to gain logistical support from Croatia, primarily in weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The links between the Muslim community in Brcko and the Croatians had gone back at least many, many months, hadn't they, before the events of April and May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I must say that we had very good relationship with the Croatian Democratic Union before the war. Those were not any particular special links. And finally, it turned out that we were not as close as we might have thought, and I can give you some facts to prove that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There was one common approach, wasn't there? In your evidence in the Jelisic case --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- you were asked about the call-up of reservists to the JNA, which had been issued to all citizens. That, of course, includes all citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, regardless of their ethnic background, and that was around the summer of 1991, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you said that, in your evidence, and I'm quoting precisely, page 1770 of the transcript in that case, that: "These reservists were called up with the intention of sending them to war in Croatia, against Croatia, and that is not what the people wanted." Now, my question is: When you say, "That's not what the people wanted," who do you mean by "the people"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the citizens of Brcko municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All the citizens of Brcko municipality or only some of them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Probably. Probably some citizens, but they were a minority, did not think that. According to my estimate, 80 per cent of the population of Brcko municipality felt that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the minority that weren't opposed to call-up and fighting against Croatia, did that minority have any particular identifiable characteristics?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I know what you are aiming at. Yes, one could say that a large majority of the Serbian population wanted to accept that. However, please bear in mind that among the Serbian citizens were also those who were opposed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But in general terms, the position was very clear, wasn't it,

utterances.speaker: MR. RAMIC
utterances.text: Those of Muslim and Croat -- well, the members of the Muslim and Croat nations, I think you can describe them, were, in general, opposed; and the Serbs were, in general, in favour of the fighting against Croatia? I don't mean that there should be fighting, but since there was fighting, they were supportive of the call-up and the JNA's action against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, will you please allow me to give you an explanation? I cannot answer in simple terms. In order for me to answer and for you to be aware of the situation that was in place at the time, you have to be aware of the following: At that moment, the people - and when I say "the people," I mean everybody - the people had still not distanced themselves along the ethnic lines. That was still not in place. Another fact was that there was a war in Croatia in which the Yugoslav People's Army was involved. This war was against Croats, and it was only logical that Croats in Brcko did not want to fight against their people there. It was also only logical that Bosniaks didn't want to go there and to lose their lives there. But it was also only logical for some Serbians not to want to go into war they didn't want themselves, and I believe this would be the correct answer. At that moment, there were still no ethnic divisions, or at least they were not that obvious or visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The way you described it in your evidence in the Jelisic case was that when the people rebelled against, this that's the calling up of reservists, when the people rebelled against this - I have to add this - the army no longer called up reservists from other ethnic groups but Serbs exclusively and the army turned into a uniethnic force. So the background to that and to your complaint there, Mr. Ramic, is basically very clear, isn't it? The rebelling was by Croats, for the reasons you give, by Muslims, but not to any significant degree by Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No, that's not how it was. Let me add, please: The army called up members of all ethnic communities. At the moment when it was known that the soldiers would be sent to Croatia to fight there, all citizens wanted to join the army, provided that the military would stay on the territory of the Brcko municipality, which is what the army did not want, because they would have been obliged to arm Croats and Muslims as well. And that is why they decided to call up only the members of the Serb community, when they decided to keep those units there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, of course, you at all times, the Muslim community, were in a clear majority, weren't you, in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you remember an occasion on which your brother, Ibrahim Ramic - and I'm talking about before the end of April 1992 - publicly addressed Serb representatives and said: According to the last census, there were 46 per cent of us in the town. God willing, on the next census, there will be over 51 per cent of us and there will be no more of you left in the town." Do you remember your brother saying something either in those words or close to those words?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I don't think that this is correct. I remember the conversation you are referring to, and he did not use those words. I remember those stories. I remember those conversations. I myself was present when this was discussed. So he did not say: "There will be no more of you left in the town." When he said that in the next census, there would be over 51 per cent of us, he was talking -- he was referring to the following: And there were representatives of all ethnic communities there, including the leader of the Serb community. He meant the following: Officially, about 44 per cent of the Muslims declared themselves as Muslims. However, there was a large percentage of those who did not declare themselves as Bosniaks. So there were at least six or seven per cent of Bosniaks who had yet to be declared as Bosniaks. And that's what he had in mind. He did not imply any war events or any unusual events. That's what he had in mind, and this was, of course, known to the people he was addressing at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This was a meeting of municipal leaders, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent sure. Actually, I don't think that it was a meeting at the municipal level. It was a meeting of the group of leaders. I don't think that the parliament was the forum for that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Anyway, you remember the conversation, and it -- whatever the precise words, it was -- there was an aggressive underlying threatening tone to your brother's remarks, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: There was no reason for that. Please, let me reiterate. We did not need to be aggressive. We were perfectly aware of the fact that we stood no chance in such a war. We knew that we would be losers in any such conflict. So I cannot agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Before the end of April 1992, were there steps taken in Brcko to reduce the number of Serbs in the police department?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: In late 1990/beginning of 1991, multi-party elections were held, and I became the president of the Brcko municipality, or the mayor. We then proceeded with establishing the government together, with the representatives of the Serb people, SDS, the representatives of the Croat people through the HDZ. So it was a mutual, common agreement that we had reached, to the effect that we would establish various structures of the government on a parity basis, and that further appointments, further employments at lower levels, would be amended or improved on the basis of the ratio. It was not that we reached a specific decision at one point in time. We just said that we would take into account the need to employ, or rather, to proceed with the appointments on the basis of the ethnic composition of the municipality. That was the agreement we had reached, and it was also to be applied to the police, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Before the fighting that you describe as breaking out at the end of April and the blowing up of the bridges, for some months since the beginning of 1992, it's right, isn't it, that the Muslim community in Brcko had erected barricades in some parts of the town?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, I need to provide explanation. At that time, that is, prior to the 1st of May, during the month of April, because there had been no barricades before that. However, in early April, certain events took place in Zvornik and Bijeljina, and the news reached us. Bijeljina is 40 kilometres away from Brcko, and many citizens of Brcko have relatives or family living there. Terrible news reached us at one point about what was going on there, and all of a sudden people became fearful as to what might happen, and they thought about what they should do. At the same time, the Yugoslav People's Army - and this had been going on for a while - started taking up strange positions. They were digging in in the surrounding area of the town. There were heavy patrols of the JNA all around the town, patrols that were accompanied by some heavy vehicles, such tanks or similar vehicles. The barracks, which is located in the centre of the town, was all of a sudden surrounded by trenches, and machine-guns were placed around the barracks, with the tubes facing the town. So obviously, it was only natural for the citizens to begin to wonder. This resulted in an incident, I admit, if this is what you're asking about. There were no barricades; however, what happened was that one patrol, one army patrol, at the end of April - it could have been on the 29th of April, according to my memory, two days before the outbreak of the war - was stopped by a group of Bosniak and Croat citizens in a suburb, and this is what happened. However, it was the military, the army, that was engaged in setting up barricades all around the town on the main approaches to the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There were barricades erected by both sides, weren't there, Mr. Ramic, Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I don't think I can agree with that statement. At that time, barricades were not erected by Serbs either. It was the army that was setting up barricades. As for the Bosniak or Muslim side, they were not erecting barricades. What they did have, though, were patrols of sorts. And this happened in late April, maybe during the last four or five days in the month of April, but not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your previous evidence in the Jelisic case --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a similar issue to the one which arose just before the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- you described how, in a conversation when you had agreed to talk with the -- and this was before the 30th of April -- agreed to talk with the SDS leaders in the municipality about a division of the municipality, and you referred to the president of the SDS, Mr. Vojinovic, and you said -- Dr. Vojinovic. And as it happens, you did specifically mention, I notice, your brother, Ibrahim Ramic, at that point. That's page 1856 of the Jelisic transcript. You said: "For example, I knew the president of the SDS pretty well, Dr. Vojinovic, my brother, Dr. Ibrahim Ramic was a colleague of his. They worked together and of course they would see each other often and talk." That's the only context in which you mentioned him there. And then you said in response to a question expressed directly to him, that's Dr. Vojinovic, why they were doing that and why they needed the Serb municipality of Brcko, which is what had been suggested, or a Serb region, he answered that that is what those who were above him required from him. And you suggested he was referring to Dr. Karadzic. And then you said: "In another conversation when we agreed to talk about a division in response to my question as to how we could carry out a division when the entire area is intermixed, three quarters of the area is covered by the Muslim people." His answer: The same president of the SDS, Vojinovic, was... if you do not want to accept that, then that will be carried out by force. He didn't say that he would be it, but he said it would be implemented by force, meaning someone would come to it. And then you said you organised a meeting where you brought them, to which you brought the main people of the HDZ, the SDS, and the SDA. There were about ten of you. Dr. Vojinovic was there. They brought maps. You said: How are you going to do this? You said -- this was just before the assembly on the 27th of April. Then you said: One of them said in response to that -- and then you said specifically: "I would not want to mention his name because of his own safety, but I can give his name. He asked me that we have a private conversation, that is to say, that is a man who did not wish me personally any evil. That is a man who knew me for many years. Mustafa, that's my name...", your name, Mr. Ramic, "... accept this, otherwise bad things are going to come out." Now, again, proceeding cautiously, Mr. Ramic, I ask you in the first place, in summary -- well, first of all, did this -- you gave your evidence in the case against Mr. Jelisic in September 1999. Would you, as a starting point, consider that the same safety reasons for not mentioning that man's name still apply now?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: This is what this man told me. Those were his exact words. He wouldn't have told me this if he had known that I would make it public. He had told me this on a confidential basis, as a friend, and I consider him to be a friend of mine. He would be in a very awkward position if this should be made public. So if now you're asking me to tell you his name, I have to ask the Court for understanding. I cannot disclose his name. But in this conversation, he really said: "Mustafa, please accept this. If you fail to accept it, if you don't accept it, a lot of evil will come out of that." I knew what he meant. I realised what the situation was and then I talked to others, and then we agreed to accept it. And that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I want to be very careful not to get into discussion and argument with you, Mr. Ramic, about matters which are not for us, you and me, to debate, but to confine myself to what you can tell us about the situation. Excuse me one second. Sorry. Just getting my page number again, Your Honour. You referred specifically to safety of this man when you gave your evidence in the Jelisic case. My question was only whether the same safety concerns apply now.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: We discussed it before the break. Yes, the same concerns apply now. And I appeal to your understanding. The area I come from is still rife with distrust, despite the fact that circumstances have changed in the meantime. I appreciate the efforts of this Tribunal to give its contribution to normalising the situation. However, the safety concerns are still present. In my assessment, the risk is still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- it seems appropriate in the light of the witness's evidence at least at this point if I'd invite the Tribunal to go into private session on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now back in open session. Mr. Stewart, could you give us an indication as far as the time of the cross-examination is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, easily, Your Honour. I have only one more question. Of course, that may give rise to two or three questions to clear it up, but I only have one more point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I suppose I could say it could take two hours, Your Honour, but I'm not going to say that. It's a short point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic, do you know of an organisation called Prosvjeta, I think is how it's pronounced?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I think the translation probably is "enlightenment," into English. Did you attend a rally under that label or under the aegis of that organisation on the 18th of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I think you spoke at that rally, didn't you? Didn't you welcome the participants publicly?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And do you remember who any of the speakers were at that -- the other speakers were at that rally?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: No. You will have to remind me, because I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you very specifically. Can you say whether or not Mr. Krajisnik was present at that rally?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA RAMIC
utterances.text: To be honest, I'm not sure. As I sit here, I'm not sure. I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Is there any need to re-examine the witness, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll ask my colleagues whether they have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I finally make up my mind on whether or not to ask any questions to the witness, could you, Mr. Stewart, explain perhaps a bit more in detail what exactly the meaning, apart from allowing you to make further inquiries, but what the direct meaning was about your questions on what happened in this village at a distance from what I read in the other testimony of this witness, of some 80 kilometres away from Brcko, the attack, casualties. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. This was the village of Sijekovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any direct link, apart from that you'd like to make whatever inquiries you'd like to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder whether I did specifically enough -- now that Your Honour mentions it, I wonder whether I did specifically enough put to the witness -- I hope I did, but having caused some nervousness now as to the participation of Muslims in the killing of a number of civilians in that village. I begin to doubt whether I put that sufficiently specifically. Perhaps, Your Honour, just, without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For me, it's of importance to know what exactly this incident or these events mean for the case of the Defence before I ask for any further details. Because I'd like to invite the witness to give any further details if there is a direct point of relevance for the case as a whole. Because if it's just that during this time attacks were not exclusively or mainly performed by one of the parties in the conflict, but that other parties also made attacks now and then, if that's the issue, I'll refrain from any further details, because that's clear even without further details. But if there's any specific relevance of exactly that incident, I'd like to know from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. No. Your Honour, so there is -- there is -- let me put it this way, and I mean of course absolutely no disrespect to those who were victims of what happened there. For the purposes of this case there is nothing special about that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, apart from that it happened and who were, in the view of the Defence, those who started the incident and who were the victims. That's the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And there is also the point, when -- and it becomes a matter of argument, when set against some of the things that this witness has said in the past about no knowledge of any such matters. But no, Your Honour is right. This is not some central incident in the case in its own terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Ramic, I have no further questions for you either. That means that this concludes your testimony in this Court. I'd like to thank you for coming a far way. I'm also thanking you for answering questions from both parties, and I'd like to wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both parties are on their feet. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There's just a matter I wanted to mention prior to the introduction of the next witness. Your Honour may recall that in relation to the 92 bis submissions, in relation to the municipality of Brcko, that the Defence had sought certain excisions, certain redactions which I don't know if Your Honour has perhaps the Defence submission before you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I haven't it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can hand up my copy. In any event, I can just go to it globally. We asked for two excisions, and when one goes to the Prosecution's reply, there's -- the Prosecution there indicated that they were prepared to agree to the second redaction proposed by the Defence but not the first. I raised with my friend this morning the fact that that redaction hadn't been made, the one that they'd agreed to, and I'm just wondering if it might be appropriate for the Chamber to deal with the question of the first redaction, which I don't think has been dealt with by the Chamber prior to the introduction of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct. We had agreed to the second requested redaction, which in the English version of his statement appears on page 8, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 -- six lines up from the bottom, and it was a statement where the witness said: "I found it ridiculous that the government would --" I can't read the rest because I've blocked it out on my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm afraid that I've still got a full copy, so I could help you out. But it's the part where you read: "I found it ridiculous that the government --" yes. I don't know whether I should read it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have omitted that statement and made that redaction on the copies now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The earlier redaction they requested, I would remind the Court that that was a proposal when we were going to bring this witness as a 92 bis, but now he's here viva voce and the Defence will have an opportunity to cross-examine him about it. We're not willing to make that redaction from his statement. He has adopted that as part of his statement and my -- I believe that when he's here he will say: "Yes, that's part of my statement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas, any further issue at this moment or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I just thought it appropriate to raise the question of the fact that there had been this Defence request, there had been a Prosecution acceptance in relation to 50 per cent of our submission, and what was proposed to be done with the latter half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let me just check whether there are any protective measures in force. There are not, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two other matters if I may before we bring in the witness, Your Honour. One, are we going to the regular time today, even though we started at 9.30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because it has to do with the schedules of those who are assisting us, and also this courtroom might be needed this afternoon. So therefore, I'd rather not -- we'll lose half an hour today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the second matter is regards the procedure with 89(F) on this witness. We went through his statement and determined that there were significant portions of his statement that weren't really relevant for this particular case, and we've gone through and blacked out paragraphs on -- and parts of paragraphs in both the B/C/S and English versions. We have numbered each paragraph, but what I did was because I wasn't sure which was the best procedure used for Defence counsel and the Court was that there is one set in which I've numbered every paragraph, even those that now are entirely blocked out, which gives us a statement which has 44 paragraphs, or, in some cases where I omitted a whole paragraph I only numbered those paragraphs where there still remained at least a sentence. And there we only have 30 paragraphs in that version. I don't know which is best for everyone to work with, because if there were some issue that the Defence wanted to raise about an omitted paragraph, it might be more helpful to have the full number because that would match up with the numbered unredacted version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
