utterances.text: Does the Defence have any clear preference for --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. Microphone again. Yes, Your Honour. I think that it, from our perspective, it makes more sense as a sort of general procedure when dealing with statements of this nature to number every paragraph including --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translations continues]... Yes. Even the blackened out ones. Yes. It is so decided, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, we will show the witness the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will show the witness, then, the one that has 44 numbered paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although many lines in black.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Fazlovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will be handed out to you now by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Fazlovic. Mr. Fazlovic, we have only 20 minutes left in this hearing, so therefore you'll be only for a short period of time in this courtroom today, but we intend to continue tomorrow. Mr. Hannis, it's up to you to follow the procedure as we agreed upon earlier on. I think it is very important that at least the identity of the witness is always clearly established at the beginning of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Fazlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could the witness be handed a copy of his statement with the redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a copy for the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The Defence should have a copy already, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the Chamber would like to know what's out and what's in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And I would like to have one marked as an exhibit, Your Honour, because I propose to move it in once we've gone through this process.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be Prosecution Exhibit number P71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, do you recognise that document that's in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us what that is, please.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: This is my statement which I gave in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to review that yesterday, to check and see if there were any corrections or additions you wanted to make to it before today's court proceedings?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had an opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you satisfied now that that's a correct and accurate version of your statement, and are you willing to confirm to the Court that that's true?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to move the admission of that exhibit at this time, and I propose to read a summary of it before I ask him some additional questions about particular paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do we have sufficient copies now? Madam Registrar, I see that -- we need, then, a -- do you have another copy? Otherwise we could miss one for the time being. That is, two documents, as a matter of fact: The English translation and the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that an English translation is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my case manager just left the courtroom to make some additional copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I also do understand that drawings are attached to the B/C/S version but not to the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although -- no. It's all English text which appears on the drawings. I see that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as a matter of fact, I would propose to just detach those drawings from his statement. They're not discussed in the text of the statement, and I don't think they're necessary for the Court to understand his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The problem is that on the back of one of the pages that might be relevant, so -- but we'll solve that at a later stage. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And if I may at this time, Your Honour, I'd like to read the summary of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The witness Jasmin Fazlovic is a Bosnian Muslim who lived in Brcko and worked there as a firefighter. On 1 May 1992, a day after the bridges on the Sava River had been blown up, a contingent of JNA soldiers from Serbia came to the fire brigade and told the witness and his colleagues that they had to remain at their place of work. These soldiers said that they were from Serbia and had been sent to prevent the outbreak of war. On about the 4th of May, 1992, a group of Serbian paramilitaries, led by Mirko Blagojevic, came to the fire station and demanded to see identification papers. The witness and his Muslim colleagues were separated and taken outside, beaten, and then taken to the police station. At the police station, the chief of police, Dragan Veselic, told the witness and his Muslim colleagues that they were going to be taken to Luka and killed. A policeman that knew the witness interceded and persuaded Veselic to let the Muslim firefighters return to work. Goran Jelisic came in during this time and asked if the witness's group was coming to the Prosvjeta Hotel with him. On their way back to the fire station, the witness saw a number of dead civilians between the Prosvjeta Hotel and the library. On 10 May, 1992, the JNA major, Milorad Sehovac, deputy commander of the local garrison, came with some soldiers to the fire station and demanded to know who had made a phone call to a part of Muslim-held territory. One of the Muslim firefighters admitted the call. Major Sehovac told a soldier to kill him. The man was taken away and this witness heard a gunshot and then Sehovac ordered the body to be taken to the JNA barracks. Ranko Cesic, a Serb acquaintance of the witness, came several times to the fire station between May and September 1992. Cesic wore a red beret and a camouflage uniform and said he was part of a special unit that was engaged in cleansing parts of town. He said they "picked up balijas from the basements" and "took them to Luka or the barracks." Cesic told about killing a local butcher and later said he had killed a lot of people. He put his gun in the witness's mouth and asked if the witness wanted to be killed. Later, when the witness asked Cesic why he had done that, the answer was: "Because you are Muslim." The witness reports that sometime in June or July 1992, all three mosques in Brcko town were destroyed by explosives within minutes of one another. When the first explosion occurred, a Serb firefighter told the witness that the other two mosques would also be blown up. When the witness went to the site of the burning wooden mosque, he saw local SDS leader Djordje Ristanic arrive and heard him complain that too much explosives had been used, thereby damaging the nearby houses and medical centre. A military officer who appeared to be in charge told the firemen to not put out the fire in the mosque but only to prevent it from spreading. The witness remained at the fire station until the 15th of September, 1992, and then hid at the home of a Serb friend until he managed to be exchanged in late October 1992. The testimony of this witness is relevant to paragraphs 17 through 21, 23, 24, and 27, and to counts 1 through 8 of the indictment. That concludes my reading of the summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And now, Your Honour, I would like to ask him a few questions regarding some of the specific paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, in paragraph 3 of your statement, you talk about an event on May 1st when JNA soldiers came to the fire station and told you you had to remain there. Can you tell the Court approximately how many soldiers were in this contingent?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately six Serb soldiers came to the fire brigade station. The remainder were deployed along the main street in the town. They all wore camouflage uniforms. They were fully armed and they were members of the regular army. We talked to them. They behaved normally. They told us that we could not go back home, that the army had come out to prevent fighting, and they kindly asked us not to leave the building, not to go out. They boasted two soldiers at the fire brigade station who guarded the water tower and the fire brigade building. Other Serb soldiers who were dressed the same, however, wore insignia, the tricolour colour, without the five-points red star, they apparently were there to clean up the street. I could see them walking up and down the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlovic, did this group tell you where they were from? Were they local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not local Serbs. One of them said that they were members of a special unit from Novi Sad. They spoke with Serbian accent, so I know for sure that they were not from our town, which, after all, is not that big, so I would have recognised at least some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was this the day after the bridges had been blown up?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was on the 1st of May, sometime around 2.00 -- between 2.00 and 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then I want to take you to paragraph 5 in your statement, where you talk about the 4th of May. Between the 1st and 4th of May, did you stay in the firehouse?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the period of time up to September, I remained in the firehouse. I was not allowed to go home. All of us Muslims were required to remain at the fire station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there times where you went out on official firefighting business during that time?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever we were called either from the police or from the barracks, we went on firefighting business, usually extinguishing fire in Muslim houses. But whenever we went there, they would tell us: "Why have you come here? Why are you extinguishing fire in these Muslim houses?" Although there were Serbs in the unit, there were Serb soldiers, and in 90 per cent of the cases, they would eventually prevent us from putting out the fire. Only if the house in question was a Muslim house, but in the vicinity of a Serb house, then they would let us protect this other house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the 4th of May, you say in your statement that another group of soldiers came to the fire station. Can you tell the Judges about that? How many were they and how were they dressed, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: Before the 4th of May, nobody mistreated us. But on the 4th of May, at around 8.00, we heard explosion coming up from the yard of the firehouse. When we looked out through the window, we saw a group consisting of 50 to 60 people, who had fired from an RPG. They then rushed into the firehouse. They first lined us up and then told us to lie down. Both Muslims and Serbs were there at the moment. And they wanted to see our identity cards, to see who was what. Then they started verbally abusing us Muslims, non-Serbs, and eventually they took us out into the yard, where the Vojvoda Mirko was. Again, these people were not originally from Brcko. They were not Brcko residents. There was Slalic [phoen], Vojvoda, then -- excuse me. Blagojevic, then Stankovic, then Captain Dragan, at least the person whom they referred as Captain Dragan. But he was -- he behaved irrationally. I don't know why they took him with them. They told us -- they accused us Muslims of being snipers and they said that we should all be killed. This person by the name of Dragan was the one in favour of that, that we should all be killed on the spot. I don't know how things eventually were decided, but at one point we were sent to the police station, where we had to walk with our hands behind our necks. They escorted us --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: There was about seven of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. This group of 50 to 60 men, can you tell us what kind of uniforms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: Some wore uniforms. Some had only the camouflage trousers or only a camouflage shirt. But at any rate, there were perhaps 20 per cent of them who wore complete uniform. The rest were dressed mixed, part civilian, part military clothes. Stanko had a helmet. I remember clearly that he had a helmet with four S's on it. Mirko Blagojevic had a military shirt on. They all had white ribbons on their shoulders. It was probably a sign of recognition, so that they could recognise themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were they all armed with some sort of weapons?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were all armed. They all had automatic weapons, RPGs, the so-called Zoljas, and metal clubs, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who appeared to be in charge of this group?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the group that actually entered the firehouse? The leader -- their commander was Mirko Blagojevic, because it was to him that they addressed themselves for everything. He located his headquarters there in the firehouse that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tell us how many firemen there were in total staying at the fire station at this time and how many were Muslims and how many were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: I think that we were five, that there were five Muslims and three Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that the total contingent, eight persons, no others?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: No, this was not the total contingent. The unit had about 20 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But it was only the eight of you present on this day?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN FAZLOVIC
utterances.text: On this day, I was on duty because we worked in shifts, and it so happened that we were on duty on that day. Several days later, two to three Serbs arrived on top of that. They joined the unit later. They also worked there, but they were not on duty on this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is would be a good point to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis. Looking at the clock, we have to adjourn. Mr. Fazlovic, we'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. So I'd like to invite you to be back, but in another courtroom. That's in Courtroom I tomorrow morning. And I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given in this courtroom until now or you're still about to give. So with no one. We'll then adjourn, unless, Ms. Loukas, you would have something.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just briefly, just after the witness is excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you perhaps escort Mr. Fazlovic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Just in relation to that matter I raised just prior to the witness coming in. That was the question of the excision/redaction. I received a copy of the newly redacted statement while the witness was giving evidence, and the full redaction was not in fact made. I would indicate that the excision agreed to began: "I found it ridiculous," and ended: "Protect himself." That first sentence has gone out but the second sentence has remained in, the sentence that ends "protect himself."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If that's correct, Your Honour, then I would ask that that change be made. I didn't realise that the second portion of that agreed upon redaction had not been made. That may be my failure to read the B/C/S adequately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that it will be checked until tomorrow morning, 9.00, and that we'll then see whether we get a new redacted one. And if you give it to the Defence just five minutes in advance so that they can check whether everything is all right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there are no further issues, we'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, Courtroom I, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of April, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
